newsitem.title: ERITREA: Sudan rebels say garrison falls, advancing on Juba.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebels say garrison falls, advancing on Juba.

text.p: Sudanese rebels said on Friday they had seized a military garrison after a failed government counter-attack and were pushing towards the southern capital of Juba.
A spokesman for the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) in the Eritrean capital Asmara said the garrison at Jambo, 80 km (50 miles) northwest of Juba, fell to rebel forces on Thursday.

"The enemy had assembled one brigade, about 1,000 men, in Jambo under Brigadier Muhammed Taib El-Sanger in a futile attempt to come behind our forces using the Jambo-Lainya road but the enemy move failed and was defeated completely," Yassir Arman told Reuters.
The rebel claim could not be independently confirmed.

Arman said National Islamic Front (NIF) government troops fled leaving behind many dead as well as two T-55 tanks and a number of other vehicles. He gave no casualty figures and said he was waiting for further details.
A coalition of forces under the military command of SPLA leader John Garang is fighting to overthrow Khartoum's Islamist government in the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) rebel coalition.
In early March fighting intensified around Juba -- the southern regional capital and immediate target of the SPLA.
"Our forces are fighting in two directions to clear all Juba strategic outposts," said Arman.
SPLA officials in Nairobi on Friday said fighting was taking place at Rokom, 60 km (40 miles) northwest of Juba.
In mid-March the SPLA captured the southern town of Yei, 160 km (100 miles) southwest of Juba near the Ugandan border and on the road leading to Zairean rebel-occupied eastern Zaire.

Garang on Tuesday said the NDA coalition had seized several northeastern districts in a new offensive aimed at cutting the road between Khartoum and the main link to the outside world at Port Sudan on the Red Sea.
The government has dismissed rebel claims to control one of the districts, Aqiq, and accused Eritrea and Ethiopia of fighting alongside rebels in the north and northeast.
Both countries deny helping the rebels, as does Uganda, which is accused of backing the SPLA from the South.

Since 1983 the SPLA has fought for independence or greater autonomy for the Christian and animist south from the Moslem and Arab north. In January it was joined by groups from northern Sudan who also want to overthrow the Islamist government.
